# OpenCloud Helm chart

Deploys [OpenCloud](https://opencloud.eu) as a single-process StatefulSet, following the layout of the official [Docker Compose project](https://github.com/opencloud-eu/opencloud-compose). Companions: the yjs collaborative-editing server (enabled by default), and optionally Radicale for CalDAV/CardDAV and Apache Tika for full-text search. Office servers, external identity providers, LDAP, S3, SMTP, virus scanners, DNS and public routing are supplied separately.

This is an early 0.x release. Template, schema and policy checks pass. The [end-to-end test](#gitops-and-validation) installs the chart on a kind cluster with Keycloak and OpenLDAP and verifies Keycloak sign-in with token-based API access, roles from the `roles` claim, users and groups from LDAP, WebDAV upload and download, CalDAV/CardDAV through Radicale, the yjs route, read-only root filesystems with every companion enabled, persistence across pod replacement, externally managed service secrets, and the migration of an initialised installation. Earlier manual runs covered built-in sign-in with OpenCloud 7.2.4 and 8.1.0 and the decomposeds3 driver against an S3-compatible server. Interactive browser sign-in, office editing with a real Collabora, virus scanning, email delivery and full-text search results remain unverified. See [operating notes](#operating-notes) before production use.

## Install

The Common dependency is vendored in `charts/`; a fresh checkout needs no dependency download. The smallest install uses the built-in identity management and keeps files on the data volume:

```sh
kubectl create namespace opencloud
kubectl --namespace opencloud create secret generic opencloud-admin \
  --from-literal=adminPassword="$(openssl rand -base64 24)"
helm upgrade --install opencloud . --namespace opencloud \
  --set domain=example.org --set admin.existingSecret=opencloud-admin \
  --set ingress.enabled=true --set ingress.className=nginx
```

OpenCloud is then served at `https://cloud.example.org`; sign in as `admin`. Set `host` for a different hostname and `externalUrl` when the public URL has a non-standard port. For a production-style install with Keycloak, S3, SMTP and Collabora, start from [examples/keycloak-s3.yaml](examples/keycloak-s3.yaml).

On the first start an init container runs `opencloud init`, which writes `/etc/opencloud/opencloud.yaml` with generated service secrets, IDs and the initial administrator password to the config volume. Later starts keep that file. **The config volume is as important as the data volume**: losing it orphans all stored data. The administrator password is only read at that first start; change it later in the web UI or with the OpenCloud CLI. To provide these values yourself instead, see [externally managed service secrets](#externally-managed-service-secrets).

## Images and credentials

All images are pinned by digest in [values.yaml](values.yaml). **Changing a tag alone does not change the image:** update the corresponding `digest`, or clear it to use the tag. This applies to `image`, `yjs.image`, `radicale.image` and `tika.image`. A nonempty `global.imageRegistry` overrides their registries; mirrors must contain all enabled images.

[Renovate](renovate.json) checks the pinned images, Bitnami Common, the CI tools and GitHub Actions weekly and opens PRs that change tag and digest together; for the main image the PR also moves `appVersion` in `Chart.yaml`. Image blocks in `values.yaml` must keep the order `registry`, `repository`, `tag`, `digest` for Renovate to match them. Install the Renovate GitHub App on the repository to enable it.

The default `image` is the rolling channel (`opencloudeu/opencloud-rolling`), which the Compose project tracks. Rolling versions only receive fixes until the next one ships, so plan to upgrade with the channel every few weeks. The production channel (`opencloudeu/opencloud`) gets backported fixes over a longer period but lags behind in features: 7.2.x has no yjs support and ignores `identity.oidc.audiences`. To use it:

```yaml
image:
  repository: opencloudeu/opencloud
  tag: "7.2.4"
  digest: "sha256:6d992ccc5f1cbc7b2a9b272ba25f879b1b159c2d7ed7f5527e09059f16295697"
yjs:
  enabled: false
```

Do not downgrade an existing installation from rolling to production: data written by a newer version may not be readable by an older one.

Prefer existing Secrets. Plain credential values are stored in Helm release history even when rendered into the chart-managed `<fullname>-env` Secret.

| Credential | Existing Secret settings |
| --- | --- |
| Initial administrator | `admin.existingSecret`, `.passwordSecretKey` |
| Internal service secrets and IDs | `serviceSecrets.existingSecret` (fixed keys; see below) |
| LDAP bind | `identity.ldap.existingSecret`, `.bindPasswordSecretKey` |
| S3 | `storage.s3.existingSecret`, `.accessKeySecretKey`, `.secretKeySecretKey` |
| SMTP | `smtp.existingSecret`, `.passwordSecretKey` |
| Metrics token | `metrics.token.existingSecret`, `.secretKey` |
| Image pulls | `global.imagePullSecrets` or each image's `pullSecrets` |

Top-level `existingSecret` adds all keys of a Secret as environment variables. `extraEnv` and `extraEnvVars` set any other [OpenCloud environment variable](https://docs.opencloud.eu/docs/admin/configuration/environment-variables); an entry with the same name as a chart-set variable replaces it.

## Identity

`identity.mode: builtin` runs OpenCloud's own LDAP (idm) and OpenID Connect provider (idp). It needs an `https://` public URL, since the built-in idp refuses other issuers.

`identity.mode: oidc` disables the built-in idp and trusts `identity.oidc.issuer`. Register a public client for the web UI (`identity.oidc.webClientId`, default `web`) and the upstream client IDs `OpenCloudDesktop`, `OpenCloudAndroid` and `OpenCloudIOS` for the apps. Roles come from the `roles` claim (see [Keycloak claims](#keycloak-claims)). On OpenCloud 8.x, set `identity.oidc.audiences` to enable access-token audience validation. The two Compose setups map as follows:

| Compose setup | Chart values |
| --- | --- |
| External IdP with autoprovisioning (`idm/external-idp.yml`) | `identity.oidc.autoprovision: true` (default). Users live in the built-in idm, or in an external LDAP with `identity.ldap.writeEnabled: true`. |
| Keycloak shared user directory (`idm/ldap-keycloak.yml`) | `identity.oidc.autoprovision: false`, `userClaim: uuid`, `userCs3Claim: userid`, and `identity.ldap` with `userSchemaId`/`groupSchemaId: entryUUID`, `disableUserMechanism: none`, `writeEnabled: false`, `serverUuid: true`. See [ci/full.yaml](ci/full.yaml). |

Setting `identity.ldap.uri` replaces the built-in idm with that directory. The chart does not deploy Keycloak or LDAP and does not create IdP clients, users or roles.

### Keycloak claims

Federating LDAP in Keycloak does not by itself put the claims OpenCloud needs into the tokens. In the shared-directory setup, configure Keycloak so that the access token and the userinfo response of every OpenCloud client carry:

- **`uuid`**: the value OpenCloud uses as the user ID, which is the LDAP attribute named in `identity.ldap.userSchemaId` (`entryUUID` above). In Keycloak, add a *user-attribute* LDAP mapper from `entryUUID` to a user attribute `uuid` (always read from LDAP), and a *User Attribute* protocol mapper from `uuid` to the claim `uuid` in a client scope assigned to the clients. Keycloak's own user ID is not the LDAP `entryUUID` unless the federation's UUID attribute makes it so; do not rely on `sub`.
- **`roles`**: a multivalued claim containing the role names. OpenCloud's default mapping turns `opencloudAdmin`, `opencloudSpaceAdmin`, `opencloudUser` and `opencloudGuest` into its admin, space admin, user and user-light roles. Grant them as realm roles, directly, through groups, or with a *role* LDAP mapper from LDAP groups, and map them with a *User Realm Role* protocol mapper to the claim `roles`. For other names set `identity.oidc.roleAssignment.mapping`; OpenCloud reads that mapping only from its config file, so the chart renders it into `proxy.yaml`.

[tests/e2e/realm.json](tests/e2e/realm.json) is a minimal working realm with these mappers, used by the end-to-end test.

## Externally managed service secrets

By default `opencloud init` generates OpenCloud's internal secrets and IDs into `/etc/opencloud/opencloud.yaml` on the config volume. For GitOps, provide them instead with `serviceSecrets.existingSecret`: the init container is skipped, nothing is generated, and every value is read from the Secret. This mode is supported with `identity.mode: oidc` and an external `identity.ldap.uri` only; the built-in idm and idp need further generated credentials and signing keys, and the chart rejects those combinations.

Create the Secret **once** per installation and store it like any other secret (SOPS, Sealed Secrets, an external secret store). Never regenerate it for an existing installation:

```sh
scripts/service-secrets.py generate --name opencloud-service-secrets > opencloud-service-secrets.yaml
```

The script uses the operating system's cryptographically secure random generator, writes random version-4 UUIDs for the IDs, and only prints; Helm never generates or rotates these values. Helm also cannot check the Secret's contents when rendering: a missing key fails at pod start, a wrong value at runtime.

| Key | Environment variable | Purpose | Changing it on an existing installation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `storageUsersMountId` | `STORAGE_USERS_MOUNT_ID`, `GATEWAY_STORAGE_USERS_MOUNT_ID` | ID of the user storage; part of the resource ID of every space and file | Never. Shares, links, favourites and desktop-client sync state refer to resources by these IDs. |
| `systemUserId` | `OC_SYSTEM_USER_ID` | ID of the internal system user that stores system metadata such as shares and settings | Keep stable; metadata created under the old ID would no longer belong to the system user. |
| `graphApplicationId` | `GRAPH_APPLICATION_ID` | Application ID that OpenCloud's app roles belong to | Keep stable; stored role assignments refer to it. |
| `serviceAccountId` | `OC_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_ID` (also the settings service's service-account list) | Account the services use to act on their own behalf | Keep stable; it holds the service-account role. |
| `serviceAccountSecret` | `OC_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_SECRET` | Credential of that account | Can be replaced; takes effect on restart. |
| `jwtSecret` | `OC_JWT_SECRET` | Signs and verifies internal access tokens | Can be replaced; tokens issued before the restart become invalid. |
| `machineAuthApiKey` | `OC_MACHINE_AUTH_API_KEY` | Authenticates internal service-to-service requests | Can be replaced; takes effect on restart. |
| `systemUserApiKey` | `OC_SYSTEM_USER_API_KEY` | Credential of the system user | Can be replaced; takes effect on restart. |
| `transferSecret` | `OC_TRANSFER_SECRET` | Signs upload and download transfer tokens | Can be replaced; transfers in progress fail. |
| `urlSigningSecret` | `OC_URL_SIGNING_SECRET` | Signs URLs, for example image downloads by the office suite | Can be replaced; already issued signed URLs stop working. |
| `wopiSecret` | `COLLABORATION_WOPI_SECRET` | Signs and encrypts WOPI tokens for the office integration | Can be replaced; open office sessions end. |
| `thumbnailsTransferToken` | `THUMBNAILS_TRANSFER_TOKEN` | Signs thumbnail download tokens | Can be replaced; takes effect on restart. |

The purposes follow the upstream configuration descriptions. Replacing the secrets in the lower part of the table has not been tested by this chart; treat any change as a maintenance operation and test it first.

With the Secret in place, `/etc/opencloud` holds no state, and `persistence.config.enabled: false` replaces its volume with an emptyDir. The chart's own files (`csp.yaml`, `proxy.yaml`, `apps.yaml` and the others) are still mounted into it read-only.

### Migrating an initialised installation

Migration is a separate operation from the switch to new values; plan a short downtime and back up both volumes first.

1. Copy the existing values into a Secret. The script refuses to write a Secret when a value is missing or the per-service copies disagree:

   ```sh
   kubectl -n opencloud exec opencloud-0 -c opencloud -- cat /etc/opencloud/opencloud.yaml \
     | scripts/service-secrets.py from-config - --name opencloud-service-secrets > opencloud-service-secrets.yaml
   ```

   Store the result like the generated variant and apply it. Keep a copy of `opencloud.yaml` until the migration is verified.
2. Upgrade with `serviceSecrets.existingSecret` and leave `persistence.config.enabled: true`. The StatefulSet keeps its volume claim templates, so the upgrade goes through in place. The old `opencloud.yaml` stays on the config volume but holds the same values.
3. Optionally drop the config volume. Volume claim templates of a StatefulSet cannot be changed in place, so recreate the StatefulSet while keeping its pods and claims, then upgrade:

   ```sh
   kubectl -n opencloud delete statefulset opencloud --cascade=orphan
   helm upgrade opencloud … --set persistence.config.enabled=false
   ```

   The new StatefulSet takes over the pod and reuses the `data-opencloud-0` claim by name. Delete the orphaned `config-opencloud-0` claim once everything works.

Both steps are covered by the end-to-end test.

## Storage

`storage.driver` selects where file content lives. Choose it before the first start: switching drivers does not migrate data.

| Driver | File content | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `posix` (default) | Data volume | Upstream default |
| `decomposed` | Data volume | The Compose project's documented default |
| `decomposeds3` | S3 bucket | Metadata stays on the data volume; set `storage.s3` |

Whatever the driver, `/var/lib/opencloud` holds the idm database, NATS JetStream, the search index, thumbnails and metadata, so `persistence.enabled: false` loses everything on pod replacement. OpenCloud runs as one replica: the single process embeds NATS and local state, and scaling out requires OpenCloud's microservice deployment, which this chart does not provide. Volumes are `ReadWriteOnce` by default; `existingClaim` adopts existing claims instead of the StatefulSet templates.

## Networking

The `<fullname>` Service serves HTTP on port 9200; terminate TLS at the Ingress or Gateway. Set a body-size limit suitable for uploads on the controller, for example `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "0"`. `gatewayAPI.httpRoute` attaches to an existing Gateway instead.

**OpenCloud calls its own public URL**: uploads, for example, go through `https://<host>/data`. The host must resolve inside the cluster to the Ingress or Gateway, with a certificate the pod trusts. Use `hostAliases` for split-horizon setups. `insecure: true` skips certificate verification and is meant only for self-signed test installs.

The proxy also serves WOPI under `/wopi` and `/collaboration`, yjs under `/yjs`, and CalDAV/CardDAV under `/caldav/`, `/carddav/` and their `.well-known` paths; no other hostnames are needed for these. `proxy.additionalRoutes` adds custom routes.

## Web office

`collaboration.enabled` runs OpenCloud's collaboration (WOPI) service in the main process and points it at `collaboration.app.url`. Deploy the office server separately, for example with the [Collabora Online chart](https://github.com/CollaboraOnline/online/tree/main/kubernetes/helm), and allow OpenCloud as WOPI host there (`aliasgroup1=https://<host>`). The chart adds the office origin to the Content Security Policy.

For Euro-Office or OnlyOffice set `collaboration.app.name`, `product: OnlyOffice` and `proofDisable: true`, and supply an app registry that makes it the default for OOXML types through `collaboration.appRegistry`. Run only one office app: there is no locking between apps.

## Optional services

| Values | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `smtp.enabled` | Email notifications. `smtp.sender` is required; the notifications service exits without it. |
| `tika.enabled` or `tika.externalUrl` | Full-text search through Apache Tika. The bundled image is the slim variant; the `-full` tags add OCR. |
| `radicale.enabled` | Personal calendar and address book per user, authenticated by the OpenCloud proxy. Data on its own volume. |
| `yjs.enabled` (default `true`) | Real-time collaborative editing in the web UI. Needs OpenCloud 8.x; disable it on the 7.2 production channel. |
| `antivirus.enabled` | Scans uploads through an external ClamAV (`clamavSocket: tcp://host:3310`) or ICAP server. Keep the scanner's stream limit at least `antivirus.maxScanSize`. |
| `web.appsConfig` | Configuration of web extensions, rendered into `apps.yaml`. Install extensions into `/var/lib/opencloud/web/assets/apps` with `extraInitContainers`. |
| `csp.extraDirectives` | Additional Content Security Policy sources, for example for web extensions that embed other sites. |

Yjs uses the Recreate deployment strategy so upgrades stop the old document server before starting its replacement. Collaborative editing briefly disconnects during upgrades while the old server flushes its documents.

## Monitoring

Health probes use `/healthz` and `/readyz` on the proxy's debug port 9205, which is always bound. The web port answers every path with the web UI, so it cannot serve as a health check. Readiness reflects the proxy only; backend services may still be starting for a few seconds after the pod turns ready.

`metrics.enabled` adds a `<fullname>-metrics` Service for `/metrics` on the same port, and `metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled` a ServiceMonitor (requires the Prometheus Operator CRDs). In single-process mode this endpoint covers all services. Set `metrics.token` to require a bearer token for `/metrics`; health endpoints stay open.

The ServiceMonitor and its authentication Secrets always live in the Helm release namespace. Configure Prometheus's `serviceMonitorNamespaceSelector` to discover that namespace and its `serviceMonitorSelector` to match the monitor's labels; Prometheus itself can stay in a separate monitoring namespace.

## Operating notes

All containers run as non-root with a read-only root filesystem, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no privilege escalation and all capabilities dropped. ServiceAccount token automounting is disabled; the chart grants no Kubernetes RBAC permissions. When Radicale is enabled, the chart installs an ingress NetworkPolicy allowing TCP port 5232 only from this release's OpenCloud server pods in the same namespace, because Radicale trusts their X-Remote-User header. This requires a network plugin that enforces NetworkPolicy; other policies must not grant broader access to Radicale, since allow rules are additive. Port 9205 also serves metrics and is reachable on the pod IP: restrict it and the other companions with your own NetworkPolicies.

Back up the config and data volumes together (and the S3 bucket with `decomposeds3`), with OpenCloud stopped or from a consistent snapshot. Check PVC retention before uninstalling, and keep release names and `fullnameOverride` stable to preserve resource and claim names. A StatefulSet does not replace a pod that crash-loops after a bad upgrade on its own; fix the values and delete the pod.

OpenCloud's requests of 250m CPU and 512Mi memory are starting points. Tune resources and probes from measured load; the startup probe allows five minutes.

## GitOps and validation

The chart has no hooks; `helm template` output is complete. Install Gateway API and ServiceMonitor CRDs before enabling those resources.

Run local checks with Helm, Python and Docker:

```sh
pip install --require-hashes -r ci/requirements.txt
scripts/render-matrix.sh
scripts/validate-manifests.sh
python3 tests/render.py
yamllint -c .yamllint.yaml Chart.yaml values.yaml ci examples policies .github
```

`tests/e2e/run.sh` runs the end-to-end test on a throwaway kind cluster with Keycloak and OpenLDAP: externally managed service secrets, Keycloak sign-in, roles, LDAP groups, uploads and downloads, every companion with read-only root filesystems, pod replacement, and the migration of an initialised installation. It needs kind and Docker, takes several minutes and is not part of CI.

CI also checks workflow syntax and the values schema. Optional local hooks are defined in `.pre-commit-config.yaml`. These checks do not establish runtime correctness or production readiness.

`policies/kyverno/` contains optional `ValidatingPolicy` resources for pod hardening, image digests and resource requests. They are not installed by the chart. They default to `Deny` and have no namespace restriction; scope them or choose audit actions before applying to a shared cluster.

## Release

Common is vendored and included in the packaged chart. Renovate opens PRs that update it together with its archive. For a manual dependency upgrade, update `Chart.yaml`, run `helm dependency update .`, and commit `Chart.lock` and the replacement archive together. `helm dependency build .` restores dependencies from the existing lock file.

Push a `vX.Y.Z` tag matching `Chart.yaml` to run CI, package the chart, publish it to `oci://ghcr.io/<owner>/charts/opencloud`, and sign its digest with cosign. Consumers can install a published version with their configured values:

```sh
helm upgrade --install opencloud oci://ghcr.io/<owner>/charts/opencloud \
  --version <X.Y.Z> --namespace opencloud -f my-values.yaml
```

Verify published signatures against the expected repository's release workflow identity and GitHub's OIDC issuer (`https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`).
